WRT Summary Description of and Rationale for Proposed Changes to Program Name Change The Department of Writing and Rhetoric’s name does not accurately and fully reflect the research work, course and degree offerings, and trajectory of the department, nor does it resonate with students.
A more representative name for the department is the “Department of Professional and Public Writing.” Furthermore, with national trends favoring professional and technical writing careers, it is imperative that students (current and prospective) and colleagues are aware of our talent and specialty in this area.
This name change is expected to help us recruit students, promote research collaborations (both within and outside the institution), develop online graduate certificate programs, and attract new hires in professional and technical communication.
We anticipate a growing need for departments with this specialization.
The U.S.
Bureau of Labor Statistics projects employment in technical writing occupations to grow 12 percent from 2020 to 2030, which is faster than the average for all occupations.
It documents the median wage for technical writers as $74,650.

As a faculty, we are well positioned for this change.
WRT faculty hold doctorates in Professional and Technical Writing and are nationally recognized, award-winning researchers in the field.
Areas of expertise include, but are not limited to, technical communication, procedural discourse, user-experience design, civic and community literacy, digital and multimodal writing, cultural rhetorics, information design, accessibility, and science communication.
The department course offerings already reflect this expertise.
The department faculty officially voted to change the department name to the “Department of Professional and Public Writing” on November 22, 2021.
Concentration Areas We are proposing two areas of concentration that capitalize on our strengths as a department and that track with career pathways, at the same time that they fulfill our goal of encouraging civic engagement: Technical Writing and Professional and Civic Writing.
Students may select three courses to fulfill a concentration area.
Note that none of the concentration areas includes the revised core courses (see below).

Consistent with College strategic plans, concentrations will provide students in the major with an opportunity to customize the major in a way that more effectively coheres with specific career objectives.
Lastly, a nine-credit or three-course sequence constitutes a concentration that will be noted on students’ transcripts.
Revised Core Requirements We are proposing new core requirements in keeping with the latest research in Writing Studies, research into student needs, the Agenda for Change, and the Academic Strategic Plan.
The proposed core reduces the number of requirements to give majors a chance to embark on courses of study best suited to their interests and career paths.
The new requirements represent vertical integration of some of the most exciting and forward-focused of our courses.
In this core, students will find an introduction to the major, an introduction to digital writing, and a capstone that will send students into the world with a professional portfolio.
Moreover, it contains courses that emphasize the Agenda for Change.

We are retiring courses that, in their current form, are considered outdated and Eurocentric by current scholars and pedagogues in the field (201* and 360).
Instead we will integrate the aspects of these courses that are still useful and relevant into the new core courses.
The new core will contain the following courses: WRT 104: Writing to Inform and Explain.
This course is our flagship first-year writing course that offers some of the most innovative pedagogy available at the university level.
The course offers an introduction to many of the advanced courses in the major.
In particular, it introduces students to digital writing, later reinforced in other courses.
It also forwards the Agenda for Change by promoting a learner-centered classroom in which all students— regardless of preparation—can succeed.
This course also forms part of the Harrington core.
WRT 235: Digital Writing and Rhetoric.
In 235, writers practice the craft of digital writing using a wide array of contemporary digital tools and multiple modes including text, images, videos, and sound, as well as spatial and gestural modes.
We introduce the theory of digital writing and support production by assigning complex digital

genres for diverse digital audiences. This newly revised course also reinforces rhetorical theory and argument in more relevant and culturally inclusive ways. WRT 371G: Write Now: Race, Resistance, and Language Justice. Language is central to racial and cultural identity. Through interdisciplinary perspectives, this course prompts students to consider how language shapes understandings of race and identity and how they can use it as a means to pursue social justice. This course (provisionally approved by the Faculty Senate) speaks directly to the University’s Action Agenda. WRT 495: Advanced Digital Writing and Rhetoric. In this capstone course, students apply cumulative knowledge to create a professional digital portfolio that they can use to secure the career of their choice. In 495, students learn advanced digital writing and rhetorical theory, as well as advanced production skills. *Note: The Public Relations, Data Science, and Computer Science programs currently list 201 as a possible elective in their core. We have spoken with the chairs/directors of these departments, and all support its removal from our course offerings. All three program leaders believe that WRT 235 or 227 would be more relevant to their majors. Film/Media Part of the Harrington School of Communication and Media (uri.edu/harrington), the Film/Media Program offers a Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) degree and a minor.
Faculty: Rebecca Romanow, Director.
Professors Healey-Jamiel, Mandel, Moore, Sama, Swift, Trimm, Walton, and Wood; Associate Professors Chadha, Echevarría, Kealhofer-Kemp, and Reyes; Assistant Professor Wyatt; Adjunct Assistant Professors Bergstrom, and Zorabedian; Teaching Professors Brown and Romanow.
The Major.
Film/Media is an interdisciplinary program offering hands-on experience in documentary, experimental, narrative, and new media production, balanced with an emphasis on international cinemas, film/media history, criticism, and theory.
Our curriculum reflects the dynamic and diverse nature of this field, approached from a perspective of film history and media theory.
Students learn to work with the evolving and overlapping technologies involved in the production of moving images (including film, digital video, 3D animation, game design, and new media), with an understanding of the broadening and globalization of their cultural and aesthetic contexts.

A wide range of courses is available to the film/media student—courses that examine the historical, theoretical, and global approaches to the analysis and creation of moving images.
The film/media program prepares students for careers in such areas as independent filmmaking; animation and media design; film and television industries; advertising, marketing, and public relations; and media criticism.
Graduates of this program are also prepared to continue with graduate studies, either in film and media production for an M.F.A., or in a master’s or doctoral program in film and media studies.
Students majoring in film/media must complete a minimum of 31 credits (maximum 46) in approved courses toward the major.
FLM 101 or FLM 101H is a required prerequisite.
All students must complete the core courses: FLM 110, FLM 203 (or ENG 302), FLM 204 (or FLM 205 or 206), including the senior-level seminar FLM 495; a minimum of 6 credits from the production and technique category and 6 credits from the critical studies category; a minimum of 3 elective credits in courses that count toward the film major (following).

This wide range of choices in film/media courses permits students to design a major that will meet both personal and professional goals.
Students must have a plan of study approved by an academic advisor in the film media program before beginning their coursework in the major.
Production and Technique: These courses focus on the different approaches to and practices of film/video production—how moving images are created, designed, and used to serve a variety of functions: ART 204, 213, 214, 215, 304, 306, 314, 315, 316; COM 316B, 341, 342, 344, 445; FLM 110, 220, 344, 351, 445, 477, 491; JOR 221, 331.
Critical Studies: These courses emphasize the important traditions of genre and the literary and aesthetic approaches toward understanding and valuing film/media, and integrates them into their broad historical, cultural, and ideological contexts: AAF 352; ART 374, 376, 377; CLS 451; COM 346, 414; ENG 205 D, 245, 300A, 300B, 302, 303, 304, 305D, 352, 451; FLM 203, 204, 205, 206, 214, 352, 444, 451, 491, 495; FRN 320; GWS 350; HIS 358; HPR 324, 411; ITL 315; JOR 311; SPA 320; THE 182.
FRN 320, ITL 315, and SPA 320 are taught in English.

Other courses may be used for this category with prior approval of the program director.
The following topics courses have been pre-approved: HPR

324 Images of Masculinity in Films, HPR 324 Rebel Images in Films, HPR 411 Film and Video Practicum, and GWS 350 Women and Film. Other film-based courses may count toward the major or the minor with the permission of the film/media program director. In order to transfer from University College for Academic Success to the College of Arts and Sciences, students must complete a minimum of 24 credits and have a GPA of 2.00 or higher. A total of 120 credits is required for graduation. At least 42 of these must be in courses numbered 300 or above. The Minor. In addition to fulfilling all the basic requirements for a minor (see Minor Fields of Study), students who declare a minor in film/media must complete 18 credit hours (at least 12 at the 200-level or higher) from those courses currently eligible to count toward the major. Courses in general education may count toward the minor. All courses must be taken for a grade except for the internship (Field Experience). It is strongly suggested that at least one course in the minor be from each of the following two approaches to film and media study: Production. These courses focus on the practices of film/video/media production, the design and creation of moving images. Criticism. These courses address critical and theoretical approaches to film/media and the broader contexts of international film history, genre, and ideology in which they are situated.

2021-2022 Online Catalog URI 2021-2022 Online Catalog About the Harrington School of Communication and Media About the Harrington School of Communication and Media Introduction Ammina Kothari, Director Nicholas Corsano, Associate Director Ann Salzarulo-McGuigan, Coordinator Located in the College of Arts and Sciences, the Harrington School of Communication and Media was established in 2008 to create a forward-thinking school of communication and media that prepares students for the rapidly evolving and increasingly globalized communication ecosystem. The Harrington School is a dynamic community of outstanding teachers, world-renowned scholars, and passionate learners committed to scholarly, practical, and professional approaches to the study and practice of communication and media in all its historical, contemporary, and future manifestations. Our faculty and students are principled professionals skilled in critically evaluating and strategically producing information, messages, and media by employing and enhancing communication theories, multimedia platforms, and traditional and cutting-edge technology. In our evolving communication

ecosystem, our graduates are equipped with the fundamental skills and abilities needed to adapt to an ever-changing communication and media landscape and possess an intellectual commitment to lifelong learning and service to the world through their communication skills and creative abilities. The school has undergraduate programs and concentrations in communication studies, film/media, journalism, public relations, sports media and communication, and writing and rhetoric. The school is also home to graduate programs in library and information studies (M.L.I.S), and an M.A. and ABM (accelerated bachelors to master’s) programs in communication studies. Communication studies also offers an Accelerated Degree Completion Online (B.A.) program. The Harrington Core The Harrington core curriculum was developed to ensure that all Harrington School graduates have a shared set of essential skills from across the contemporary communication and media landscape, and is required for students in each of the six undergraduate majors. The core curriculum reflects the unique contributions that each program makes to our understanding of communication and media. Beyond fulfilling many of the core requirements in general education, the Harrington core provides students with the unique opportunity to develop and enhance their digital media production skills via the Production and Presentation Fundamentals (SCM 105) requirement; competencies that are essential and applicable across a wide variety of industries and careers. Lastly, the core curriculum recognizes the value of interdisciplinary education for all Harrington students.
